explanations.explanation: Paul, an apostle writing to the believers in Ephesus (Ephesians 1:1), says, “…I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received…” He writes this as a prisoner, and he calls himself an ambassador in chains (Ephesians 6:20). I think that gives his words extra weight. A man in chains is asking about the walk, not the view.

Not here, friend. Paul calls himself a prisoner in the Lord, then moves straight to urging them to walk in a manner worthy of the calling they have received. Most of us would open with "so, about getting me out of here." Paul's mind is on how they live.

Paul doesn't ask for visitors in this verse. He says he's a prisoner in the Lord, then urges them to walk in a manner worthy of the calling they have received. His request is about how they live, not where he is. I think he wants them to keep their eyes on the calling.

Verse 2 opens the list with “…all humility and gentleness…” Those two come first, and patience follows. Friend, humble and gentle sounds quiet, but a gentle person in a heated moment is the loudest thing in the room. That's a worthy walk.

Those two aren't on Paul's list. Verse 2 gives humility, gentleness, patience, and bearing with one another in love. I know courage and strength sound impressive, like a hero in a movie trailer. Paul's list is quieter than that, but it takes plenty of strength to live out.

Good qualities, but they aren't in this verse. Paul lists humility and gentleness, then patience, then bearing with one another in love. Those are the ones he puts on the table here. Joy is welcome at my bakery any day, but it isn't on this list.

Yes, baker. Right after humility and gentleness, Paul writes “with patience.” It's one of the things he lists for a worthy walk. Patience is the one I have to practice every time a batch is in the oven and my mustache itches to open the door.

This one is true. Paul writes “…with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love…” Patience sits right in the middle of his list. I'd have loved to skip it, friend, but there it is.

Paul says, “…with diligence to preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace.” Notice he says preserve. The unity is already there, and the job is to guard it with diligence. It's like a fresh batch cooling on the rack: you don't have to make it again, you just have to keep hands and elbows off it.

Paul doesn't say that here. What he tells them to preserve with diligence is the unity of the Spirit, through the bond of peace. Customs can be dear to people, but they aren't what this verse is about. His focus is on the Spirit's unity.

That isn't in the verse, friend. Paul says to put in diligence to preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace. He's talking about the believers together, not a building. The thing worth guarding here is their unity.

Paul doesn't say that. He says to preserve the unity of the Spirit “…through the bond of peace.” Peace is the bond, not a rulebook. A bond of peace holds people together, and a long list of rules doesn't do that.
Right, baker. Paul says the unity of the Spirit is kept “…through the bond of peace.” Strict rules don't show up anywhere in that verse. Peace is what holds it together.

Paul says, “There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called…” One hope, friend. Everybody in the body is headed toward the same one. That means nobody has to hunt for their own.

Paul says the opposite. Everything in these verses is "one": one body, one Spirit, and they were called to one hope. Many paths would sound nice and roomy, but it's not what he writes. One hope is the number he gives.

Not in this verse, baker. Paul says they were called to one hope when they were called. He puts it right beside one body and one Spirit. Separate callings aren't in the verse, and gifts don't get handed out until later in the passage.

explanations.answer: Over all and through all and in all
explanations.explanation: Paul describes the one God and Father of all as the One “…who is over all and through all and in all.” Over, through and in, friend. Three little words, and I find them comforting.

explanations.answer: Far above all and apart from all
explanations.explanation: Half of that is close, since Paul does say He is over all. But he doesn't stop there. He says God is “…over all and through all and in all.” Nothing in the verse says apart from all.
That's not what Paul writes. He calls Him the one God and Father of all, who is “…over all and through all and in all.” The word he keeps using is all. Nothing in the verse limits it to a few.

Paul says, “Now to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ.” Each one, baker. Paul counts himself in that "us," and a stamper from the back of a junk drawer happily does too.

Paul never mentions earning in this verse. He says grace has been given to each one of us, according to the measure of the gift of Christ. Grace is given, and that's what makes it grace. No timecard required.
That's not what the verse says. Paul writes that grace has been given “…to each one of us…” No ranking by strength of faith is in there. The measure he names is the gift of Christ.

Paul says the One who descended is the very One who ascended above all the heavens, “…in order to fill all things.” So going up had a purpose, and the purpose was filling. Friend, I think of it like a bakery with the oven on. The warmth reaches every corner.
Paul gives a different reason. He says the One who ascended did it “…in order to fill all things.” The verse gives the reason, and leaving the earth behind isn't it.

I'd have guessed a nap too, friend, but that's not the reason Paul gives. He says the One who ascended above all the heavens did it “…in order to fill all things.” Resting doesn't appear in the verse, and filling does.

Verse 11 says, “And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers…” So apostles and prophets are the first two on the list. Evangelists, pastors and teachers follow right behind them, baker.
Those two aren't on Paul's list. Verse 11 names apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers. Kings and priests never show up in the verse. Paul's list is about people given to the body.
Not in this verse, friend. Paul lists apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers. Judges and elders don't appear in it. Checking a list against the text is a good habit, baker.

Yes, baker. Paul says He gave them “…to equip the saints for works of ministry…” Equip means getting people ready to do the work. A good leader hands you the tools and then trusts your hands to use them.

Close to what some might guess, but Paul's word is equip. He says these people were given “…to equip the saints for works of ministry…” Governing isn't the job in this verse. The saints are being readied to do the work.
Paul doesn't use that word here. The verse says they were given “…to equip the saints for works of ministry…” Equip is the job. Nothing in the verse puts these leaders in a judge's seat.

Right, baker. Verse 12 says they're given “…to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ…” Equipping and building up go together in the same sentence. The body of Christ is what's being built.

Plot twist, baker: that one is true. Paul says they were given to equip the saints for works of ministry and “…to build up the body of Christ…” Building up is right there in the purpose, plain as flour on an apron.

Paul says no such thing. He says the building goes on “…until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God…” Having enough leaders isn't the finish line. The finish is unity, knowing the Son of God, and maturing.

Right, baker. Paul says it continues “…until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God, as we mature to the full measure of the stature of Christ.” Leaders aren't a stopping point. The goal is much bigger than a headcount.

Paul says, “Then we will no longer be infants, tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching…” He's talking about growing up into maturity. I'll say it plain, friend: nobody's embarrassed to have been an infant once. The point is to keep growing.

Paul's word is infants, not rebels. He says that once we mature, we will no longer be infants, tossed about by the waves. His picture is about growing up, not about rebelling. Rebels isn't in this verse.

Close in feeling, since being tossed about sounds a bit like wandering. But the word Paul uses is infants. He says, “Then we will no longer be infants, tossed about by the waves…” The picture is of someone not yet grown up.

Paul doesn't call it harmless. He says infants are “…tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching…” Then he adds “…the clever cunning of men in their deceitful scheming.” That doesn't sound harmless, baker.

Right, baker. Paul describes believers who aren't mature as “…tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching…” He also mentions “…the clever cunning of men in their deceitful scheming.” He never calls any of it harmless.

Paul says, “Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will in all things grow up into Christ Himself, who is the head.” Paul puts truth and love together in one phrase, friend. Speaking the truth is the job, and love is how he says to do it.
That isn't Paul's way. He says, “…speaking the truth in love…” Anger isn't in the verse. Love is the way the truth is spoken.
Paul doesn't say that. He says to speak “…the truth in love…” Nothing about secrecy is in the verse. Speaking the truth is the job, and love is how he says to do it.

Paul says we grow up into Christ Himself, “…who is the head.” The body grows up into the head. I think that's a picture worth keeping, baker, since everything else in the body takes its direction from the head.
Paul's word is head, not hand. He says Christ Himself “…is the head.” Hands are great, and mine are made of mustache, but the verse names the head. Everything else in the body grows up into Him.
Paul doesn't call Christ the foot. He says Christ Himself “…is the head.” The body grows up into Him. Feet matter, but the head is the word in this verse.

explanations.answer: The work of each individual part
explanations.explanation: Paul says the whole body “…grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part.” Each part, baker, not just a few. I'm just a small stamper, and I'd say that's good news.

explanations.answer: The work of its leaders only
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't limit it to leaders. He says the body builds itself up in love “…through the work of each individual part.” Leaders are given to equip the saints, and the saints do works of ministry (Ephesians 4:12). So the work belongs to every part.

explanations.answer: The strength of its biggest parts
explanations.explanation: That's not what the verse says. Paul says the body grows “…through the work of each individual part.” He doesn't rank parts by size. Every part counts, even the small ones, friend.
